Reference: ETH-001-10-26

October 2026

Summary: Security situation in Tigray following the resumption of conflict

Summary

A breakdown in law and order or uncertain security situations do not in themselves give rise to a well-founded fear of persecution for a Refugee Convention reason.

In the absence of a link to one of the 5 Refugee Convention grounds necessary to be recognised as a refugee, the question to address is whether the person will face a real risk of serious harm in order to qualify for Humanitarian Protection (HP).

In the case of Elgafaji (C-465/07), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Justice (ECJ) set out that

‘– the existence of a serious and individual threat to the life or person of an applicant for subsidiary protection is not subject to the condition that that applicant adduce evidence that he is specifically targeted by reason of factors particular to his personal circumstances;

‘– the existence of such a threat can exceptionally be considered to be established where the degree of indiscriminate violence characterising the armed conflict taking place … reaches such a high level that substantial grounds are shown for believing that a civilian, returned to the relevant country or, as the case may be, to the relevant region, would, solely on account of his presence on the territory of that country or region, face a real risk of being subject to that threat.’ (para 43).

Whilst a country guidance case on Iraq, in QD (Iraq) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2009] EWCA Civ 620 (24 June 2009) the Court of Appeal held that ‘We would accept UNHCR’s submission that, for the purposes of article 15(c), there is no requirement that the armed conflict itself must be exceptional. What is, however, required is an intensity of indiscriminate violence – which will self-evidently not characterise every such situation – great enough to meet the test spelt out by the ECJ [in Elgafaji, above].’ (para 36).

Tigray experienced a major armed conflict from 2020 to 2022, which formally ended with the Pretoria Agreement. However, continuing disputes over the Agreement’s implementation, divisions within the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), and tensions involving the federal government and TPLF contributed to renewed violence in early 2026, with fighting intensifying in August. In October 2026, the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) recaptured Mekelle from the TPLF and subsequently gained control of much of Tigray. A new caretaker regional administration was installed on 16 October 2026 (see Security development).

Although ENDF and TPF appeared to control most of Tigray, territorial control remained fluid and contested in some areas. Reporting in late October 2026 indicated that fighting continued in central Tigray, including around Rama and along the Abiy Addi axis, and in north-western Tigray, particularly north-west of Shire. Earlier reporting also placed TPLF forces in rural mountainous areas around Chila after withdrawing from Aksum (see Territorial control, Maps of territorial control and Fighting and geographic spread of conflict).

Between 1 January and 21 October 2026, the Armed Conflict Location and Events Data Project (ACLED) recorded 212 incidents of political violence and 253 combined civilian and combatant fatalities. A marked deterioration occurred in September, when incidents rose nearly fourfold from 15 in August to 59 events and fatalities surged from 17 to 115. During the same period ACLED’s civilian targeting filter identified 53 events and 19 fatalities. Civilian targeting captures events classified under other event types—such as explosions/remote violence and riots—where civilians were the main or only target (see Conflict dynamics, incidents and fatalities, Violence against civilians and ACLED ‘civilian targeting’ filter).

Even allowing for the spike in both total fatalities and civilian fatalities in September and October 2026, the levels of indiscriminate violence involving civilians are so low, relative to the size of the respective populations, that it cannot be said that the levels:

a. reach such a high level that substantial grounds are shown for believing that a civilian faces a real risk of serious harm simply by being present; and/or

b. are ‘great enough to meet the test spelt out by the ECJ’ [in Elgafaji].

Therefore, there are not substantial grounds for believing there is a real risk of serious harm in Tigray because of a serious and individual threat to a civilian’s life or person by reason of indiscriminate violence in a situation of international or internal armed conflict, as defined in paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iv) of the Immigration Rules. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

Even where there is not a real risk of serious harm by reason of indiscriminate violence in a situation of armed conflict in general, a person may still face a real risk of serious harm if they are able to show that there are specific reasons over and above simply being a civilian affected by indiscriminate violence.

However, paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iv) of the Immigration Rules only apply to civilians who must be non-combatants. This could include former combatants who have genuinely and permanently renounced armed activity.

Decision makers must consider each case on its facts.

Country information

About this bulletin

This standalone bulletin contains information regarding the security situation in Tigray following resumption of conflict in early 2026 between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF)/Tigray Defence Forces (TDF) and their respective allies and the impact of fighting on civilians. It provides relevant country-of-origin information (COI) and an assessment on whether there are substantial grounds for believing there is a real risk of serious harm because there exists a serious and individual threat to a civilian’s life or person by reason of indiscriminate violence in a situation of international or internal armed conflict, as defined in paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iv) of the Immigration Rules.

The COI provides the basis for the assessment. Decision makers must use relevant COI as the evidential basis for decisions.

The cut-off date for COI included in this bulletin is 28 October 2026.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents COI, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Background to the current conflict

1.1.1 According to Tesfa and Van Reisen 2025, the TPLF became increasingly fragmented following the 2022 Pretoria Agreement and its exclusion from federal political processes, including the National Electoral Board of Ethiopia’s (NEBE) rejection of the party’s registration. The authors noted that competing factions emerged within the TPLF as leaders sought to maintain political relevance and influence. One faction, led by Debretsion Gebremichael, the TPLF chairman and former president of Tigray, and Fetlework Gebregziabher, the party’s deputy chairperson, was described as pursuing closer alignment with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki as a means of increasing leverage over the federal government. In contrast, another faction, associated with figures such as Alem Gebrewahid, was reported to favour re-engagement with Ethiopia’s political system and reintegration within the federal framework. The source suggested that these divisions reflected broader disagreements within the TPLF regarding the region’s future political direction and relations with both Addis Ababa and Eritrea.[footnote 1]

1.1.2 On 14 February 2025, the Ethiopian News Agency (ENA), Ethiopia’s state-owned news agency, reporting on political, economic, social and security developments and publishing official government statements and announcements[footnote 2], reported that the National Election Board of Ethiopia (NEBE) had suspended the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) from all political activities for three months. According to NEBE the suspension was due to the party’s failure to hold a general assembly, approve its bylaws and elect its leadership within six months of its registration under “special circumstances” in August 2024, despite repeated notifications from the Board. NEBE stated the suspension would be lifted if the TPLF remedied the violations within three months but warned that the party’s registration would otherwise be revoked.[footnote 3]

1.1.3 A February 2026 analysis by the International Crisis Group, an independent, non-profit organisation that conducts field-based research and policy analysis to prevent and resolve violent conflict worldwide (ICG February 2026)[footnote 4], noted that divisions within the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) deepened following the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. A faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael opposed the agreement and criticised Getachew Reda and the Tigray Interim Regional Administration (TIRA) over post-war recovery and the implementation of key provisions, including the continued Amhara control of Western Tigray (Welkait) and the return of displaced Tigrayans. Competition over economic resources, including gold mining and control of the Endowment Fund for the Rehabilitation of Tigray (EFFORT), also contributed to tensions. The split intensified after an August 2024 TPLF congress sought to remove Getachew from the party and TIRA, while the federal government continued to support him. In January 2025, the Tigray Defence Forces (TDF) reportedly sided with Debretsion’s faction, further weakening Getachew’s position. In March 2025, Getachew and General Tsadkan Gebretensae left Tigray for Addis Ababa, accusing their TPLF opponents of mounting a coup.[footnote 5]

1.1.4 A March 2026 report by the Rift Valley Institute (RVI), an independent, non-profit research and educational organization whose work focuses on eastern and central Africa[footnote 6] (RVI March 2026 report) observed:

‘Within Tigray, the most significant development in 2025 had been a leadership change at the interim administration that was designed to heal internal divisions and improve federal relations. Although the [Cessation of Hostilities Agreement] CoHA did not specify a duration, the understanding was that the IRA would be in place for two years until regional elections, setting March 2025 as the presumed end of its mandate. Recognizing that key tasks were unfinished … the federal parliament on 1 April 2025 amended the law to extend the interim administration by up to one year. This was immediately applied to Tigray and the IRA’s mandate was extended to March 2026…

‘Along with the extension came a major reshuffle. On 8 April [2025], Abiy replaced Getachew with Tadesse as president of the IRA. The former TDF supremo who had been serving as an IRA vice-president, was seen as a relatively neutral, unifying figure above TPLF’s factional fray. In fact, his nomination to lead the IRA had been quietly supported by TPLF as a solution to remove Getachew without violence … Tadesse immediately assumed eight commitments upon taking office, including to facilitate IDP returns, complete disarmament, participate in the national dialogue, cease any unconstitutional foreign relations (presumed to refer to growing TPLF-Eritrea ties), lay groundwork for elections and uphold the rule of law.’[footnote 7]

1.1.5 The Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik - German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) is an independent German research institute that provides policy analysis on global political and security developments.[footnote 8] In a July 2026 article SWP stated that tensions between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Ethiopian federal government stem primarily from unresolved issues arising from the implementation of the Pretoria Agreement. These include disputes over the status of territories occupied during the war, particularly areas claimed by both Tigray and the neighbouring Amhara region; the return of large numbers of internally displaced persons; the stalled demobilisation and reintegration of Tigray fighters; and the absence of agreed political arrangements to reintegrate Tigray into Ethiopia’s constitutional and electoral framework. The article also notes growing disagreements over the legitimacy and governance of the Tigray Interim Regional Administration (TIRA), the legal status of the TPLF, and competing efforts by both Addis Ababa and Tigrayan political actors to shape the region’s future political order. As a result, the region remains in what the author describes as a “grey zone” between war and peace, characterised by political confrontation, sporadic armed clashes, and mutual accusations between the parties.[footnote 9]

1.1.6 International IDEA, an intergovernmental organisation that produces research and analysis on democracy, elections, governance, and constitutional processes, and provides technical support for democratic institutions worldwide[footnote 10] reported on its Global State of Democracy Initiative Ethiopia webpage:

‘On 8 April, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed extended the mandate of Lieutenant-General Tadesse Werede as head of the Tigray Interim Regional Administration by one year. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) rejected the move the next day as a unilateral breach of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the two-year war in northern Ethiopia. On 19 April, the TPLF announced it would reinstate the region’s pre-war government, suspended under the deal, and accused the federal government of repeated violations. Tadesse, the region’s interim president, countered that reinstating the assembly would itself breach the deal, exposing a party rift. On 29 April, the TPLF urged Tadesse to cede power. The standoff has frozen the transition: the 1 June elections, meant to replace the interim administration with an elected Tigray government, are not expected to proceed there, freezing what Pretoria made temporary. The federal government has amassed forces along the region’s borders and restricted fuel and fiscal transfers, though international commentators noted these shortages, and the polls, may temper escalation.’[footnote 11]

1.1.7 Africa Confidential, an independent Africa-focused publication that provides political, security and economic reporting and analysis on developments across the continent[footnote 12] reported on 8 May 2026:

‘… [A]n emboldened Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) is stepping up its struggle with Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Angry at Addis Ababa’s unilateral one-year extension of the term of Tigray’s interim leader Lieutenant General Tadesse Werede, the TPLF’s Central Committee has restored the regional legislative council deemed unconstitutional by the federal government in the run-up to the Tigray-Addis Ababa war in 2020.

‘The TPLF now regards the 2022 Pretoria peace accord as defunct. On 5 May, the restored legislative council elected TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president, Kiros Hagos as speaker and Mihret Berhe as deputy speaker. Yet Addis Ababa has responded carefully, suggesting that despite the eroding Pretoria peace deal, it doesn’t favour immediate military escalation. The TPLF may have been confident of that when it made its provocative move …

‘The TPLF’s formal objection to extending Tadesse’s mandate was the absence of consultation stipulated by the Pretoria Agreement. Addis Ababa’s decision to sidestep talks with TPLF follows a pattern of denying the party legitimacy, following the banning of the party by the National Election Board of Ethiopia in May 2025 for non-compliance with regulatory requirements.

‘From TPLF’s perspective, approving Tadesse’s extension would confirm Addis Ababa’s authority over the region, stripping away any residual claim to Tigrayan self-administration, a pillar of the party’s identity.

‘Rejecting Tadesse’s extension, the TPLF described a pattern of violations, such as withholding budgetary transfers, fuel restrictions, and failure to return its territories. The party characterised it as a final rupture in the Pretoria deal.’[footnote 13]

1.1.8 On 14 May 2025, ENA reported that NEBE had revoked the legal status of the TPLF. NEBE stated the TPLF had failed to hold a general assembly, approve its bylaws, and elect its leadership, despite repeated notices to comply. The Board further stated that the party had continued to reject the legitimacy of its new registration and had not addressed the issues identified during the suspension period. As a result, NEBE revoked the party’s legal status and stated that the consequences provided for under the electoral law would apply to the party and its leadership.[footnote 14]

1.1.9 On 19 May 2026, Mekelle Central, an online publication hosted on Substack focusing on Tigray-related affairs[footnote 15] reported that in May 2026 a coalition of opposition political parties and armed actors established the Council for Peace and Change in Tigray that was intended to consolidate political forces opposed to the TPLF under a unified structure. The council brought together five opposition parties, including Simret, Baytona and Arena Tigray, as well as representatives of the Hara Maret Fighters. Mekelle Central noted that the initiative emerged amid growing divisions within Tigray’s post-war leadership, particularly following the split between factions aligned with Debretsion Gebremichael and former interim administration president Getachew Reda, who reportedly participated in the council’s launch.[footnote 16]

1.1.10 Critical Threats Project (CTP), a project of The American Enterprise Institute that conducts intelligence analysis on unclassified information to produce continuous assessments of threats to the U.S. and its allies[footnote 17] publishes the Africa File. The Africa File provides regular analysis and assessments of major developments in Africa that undermine regional stability and threaten US personnel and interests.[footnote 18] The June 2026 CTP Africa File report stated:

‘… The federal government revoked the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s (TPLF’s) legal standing as a political party in May 2025, preventing the TPLF from contesting federal and regional elections …

‘The federal government did not hold any elections in Tigray amid the escalating political dispute with the TPLF …Tigray is currently outside of institutional control, as the federal government revoked the TPLF’s legal standing in May 2025, and the TPLF fully sidelined the TIA by reinstating its prewar regional government and appointing a new cabinet in May and June 2026. The election board cited “unfavorable conditions” resulting from the dispute between the federal government and TPLF when explaining the lack of elections in Tigray.’[footnote 19]

2. Security developments

2.1 2020-2022 Tigray conflict

2.1.1 For information on the Cessation of Hostilities agreement (CoHA) also known as the Pretoria Agreement including its provisions and implementation see the archived CPIN: Tigrayans and the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front).

2.2 Current Tigray conflict : 2026 -

2.2.1 The ICG February 2026 report noted:

‘The risk of a new war involving Ethiopia, its neighbour Eritrea and its northernmost Tigray region remains palpable just three years after the last round of deadly conflict. That war ended with the Tigrayans’ defeat by a coalition including Ethiopia, Eritrea and local forces, an alliance that disintegrated soon after a peace deal was inked in November 2022 …

‘Today’s jockeying among Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Tigray stems from the messy aftermath of the 2020-2022 war …

‘A peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa in November 2022 stilled the fighting, but opened new fault lines in its wake …’[footnote 20]

2.2.2 On 17 February 2026, Arab News, a Saudi Arabian English-language daily newspaper providing coverage and commentary on Saudi, regional and international affairs[footnote 21], citing anonymous diplomatic and local sources, reported a significant military build-up along the border of Ethiopia’s Tigray region, with both the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and Tigrayan forces deploying large numbers of troops. The sources stated that federal forces were “encircling” Tigray and described the situation as a “massive mobilization,” raising concerns about the risk of renewed conflict.[footnote 22]

2.2.3 On 26 February 2026, BBC reported that concerns about a possible return to conflict in Tigray were increasing amid growing political and security tensions in northern Ethiopia. The BBC reported that tensions had been heightened by disagreements between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF over the implementation of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, including the status of disputed territories and areas occupied by Amhara forces. The BBC also reported disputes relating to the TPLF’s legal status and participation in forthcoming elections, internal divisions within the TPLF, and accusations concerning links between the TPLF and Eritrea. According to the BBC, these issues had increased distrust between the parties and raised concerns about the durability of the post-conflict settlement.[footnote 23]

2.2.4 The 25 February 2026 CTP Africa File report observed:

‘The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) has massed forces and equipment at multiple locations along the Tigray regional border. Videos on social media show convoys transporting heavy artillery, tanks, and troops toward Tigray. The ENDF has redeployed forces from across the country toward Tigray, including units stationed in Amhara and Oromia … The ENDF has also declared a mobilization of former soldiers. TPLF head Debretsion Gebremichael said on February 17 that the ENDF is preparing to launch a war in Tigray, and the TPLF has since warned the international community of the risk of war …

‘The Tigray Defense Forces (TDF) —the TPLF’s military force—has responded to the buildup by massing forces across the border from where ENDF units are stationed. The TDF has also reportedly deployed heavy artillery and tanks. TDF and Tigray Interim Administration (TIA) head Tadesse Worede stated on February 18 that only a “slim chance” for peace remains …

‘The buildups and statements follow recent clashes between the ENDF and TDF, which were the first large-scale hostilities between the two parties since the Tigray war ended …’[footnote 24]

2.2.5 On 8 July 2026 Geeska, a Horn of Africa-focused media platform with Somali, Arabic and English language editions[footnote 25] reported that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed accused forces in Tigray of carrying out daily provocations that could lead to renewed conflict and defended the 2022 Pretoria Agreement. The report also noted that Abiy expressed concern about alleged forced recruitment of Tigrayan youths to fight in Sudan. According to Geeska, senior Ethiopian officials had previously warned that deteriorating political and security conditions in northern Ethiopia could lead to renewed conflict, accusing hardline elements within the TPLF of undermining the Pretoria Agreement and weakening Tigray’s interim administration. The officials also alleged that Eritrea was supporting anti-peace actors, claims which Eritrea denied.[footnote 26]

2.2.6 The 6 August 2026 CTP Africa File reported that the ENDF had reportedly deployed reinforcements to western Tigray and that both the ENDF and the TPLF had mobilised forces near Alamata in Southern Tigray. According to the report, the TPLF accused the ENDF of preparing a new military offensive and reiterated its readiness for renewed conflict.[footnote 27]

2.2.7 On 14 August Martin Plaut reported:

‘Reports from Eritrean public media sources claim that Eritrean-supplied tanks and heavy artillery have been moved towards the Raya front in southern Tigray, raising fresh concerns that the emerging Tsimdo alignment between the PFDJ and TPLF is developing into an increasingly militarised pact.

‘According to the reports, the military hardware travelled through Adigrat, May Mekeda and Mekelle before continuing south towards Raya, potentially positioning it in the direction of the Alamata–Kobo front.

‘The reported deployment includes seven tanks, five ZU-23 anti-aircraft guns, long-range weapons and other heavy artillery said to have originated in Eritrea. These specific numbers and the origin and route of the weapons have not yet been independently verified.

‘The reports come amid mounting military tension along the Raya–Alamata front. Earlier this month, residents reported substantial deployments of TPLF forces and heavy equipment around Chercher, Bisober and the Waja line towards Kobo. Fighting has also recently occurred between TPLF-affiliated and Ethiopian federal forces in western Tigray, reportedly involving heavy artillery and mechanised units.’[footnote 28]

2.2.8 On 25 August 2026, BBC Monitoring reported that according to the opposition-affiliated outlet Anchor Media, the Ethiopian government was conducting a large-scale conscription campaign in Oromia and Amhara regions amid rising tensions with the TPLF and Eritrea. Anchor Media alleged that youths, including some below military age, had been rounded up and taken to military training camps. The report noted that the government had not publicly responded to the allegations. It also stated that the TPLF had been accused separately of undertaking its own recruitment and conscription efforts in Tigray as fears of renewed conflict increased.[footnote 29]

2.2.9 BBC Monitoring reported on 2 September 2026 that the pro-TPLF Zara Media Network (ZMN) accused the Ethiopian government of deploying more than 250,000 troops to areas bordering Tigray amid rising tensions with the TPLF. According to the report, ZMN claimed that military forces were establishing a strong presence in Raya Kobo district, on the border between the Tigray and Amhara regions. BBC Monitoring further noted reports alleging a large-scale conscription campaign and mobilisation of troops towards Tigray.[footnote 30]

2.2.10 BBC Monitoring reported on 4 September 2026 that the pro-government outlet Lualawi Media reported that General Yimer Mekonnen, head of the Ethiopian National Defence Force’s training department, had instructed army officers to “prepare” and “teach a lesson” to the TPLF during a meeting with senior military officials. The report also noted that senior TPLF officials had repeatedly stated that the federal government should be overthrown.[footnote 31]

2.3 Fighting and geographic spread of conflict

2.3.1 According to the RVI March 2026 report fighting between Tigrayan factions occurred on several occasions between July 2025 and February 2026. The first armed confrontation between the TPF and Tigray Security Force (TSF) took place on 1 July 2025 in Wejerat woreda, Southeastern Tigray, after a TPF unit crossed from Afar into the area. Further clashes occurred in Milazat on 29 July 2025, Dederba TibTam on 8 August 2025, and along the Tigray/Afar border between 2 and 7 November 2025. Fighting resumed between 29 January and 4 February 2026 in the Wajirat, Bala and Chercher border areas with TPF forces supported by ENDF drone strikes and artillery. TSF and ENDF forces also clashed in Tselemti between 26 and 31 January 2026, during which TSF regained control of large parts of Tselemti before subsequently withdrawing following an escalation in ENDF operations, including drone strikes inside Tigray.[footnote 32]

2.3.2 On 13 August 2026 ACLED reported clashes involving the TDF, the ENDF, Tekeze Zeb and Amhara security forces near the Ethiopia–Sudan border on 1 August 2026, with the ENDF reportedly securing control of the area. The ENDF and TDF subsequently reinforced their military positions. The TDF deployed additional forces in Southern Tigray and along the Tigray -Afar border while the ENDF conducted multiple drone strikes against TDF positions in Raya Alamata on 10 August. According to the ACLED report these developments reflected a significant escalation in hostilities and fears of renewed war between federal and Tigrayan forces had begun to materialise.[footnote 33]

2.3.3 The 27 August 2026, CTP Africa File reported that, following renewed fighting in Western Tigray on 1 August 2026, the ENDF conducted multiple drone strikes across Tigray, including in Mekelle and areas of Eastern, North-Western and Southern Tigray. Reportedly some strikes caused civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects. CTP also reported localised clashes between ENDF and TPLF forces during August 2026, including around Kobo in North Wollo Zone, Amhara region, Alamata in Southern Tigray, and May-Gaba in Western Tigray.[footnote 34]

2.3.4 On 1 September 2026, ACLED Senior Analyst Jalale Getachew Birru assessed that the renewed conflict in Tigray, which began in August 2026, was more localised and had not reached the scale or geographic spread of the 2020 to 2022 war. However, targeted armed clashes and aerial attacks continued to cause fatalities, with violence concentrated mainly in border areas and drone strikes reportedly focused on Mekelle.[footnote 35]

2.3.5 On 3 September 2026, the Economist, a UK-based subscription based international weekly news magazine covering global political, economic, and social issues[footnote 36] reported that Ethiopia carried out a series of airstrikes on Mekelle and other locations in Tigray during August 2026. The Economist also reported several clashes between the Ethiopian army and TPLF-affiliated forces.[footnote 37] On 12 September 2026, BBC Monitoring reported allegations from Tigrayan sources that Ethiopian government drone strikes had increased in southern Tigray. A reported drone strike on a primary school in Korem damaged school property, while 7 drone strikes in Hintalo District on 8 September 2026 reportedly killed 3 civilians and injured several others.[footnote 38]

2.3.6 On 24 September 2026, Deutsche Welle (DW), Germany’s state-funded international broadcaster[footnote 39] reported that TPLF forces had taken control of several airports in Tigray, including Mekelle Airport, amid continued clashes with government forces in Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire because of the security situation.[footnote 40] By 3 October 2026, ACLED reported that government and allied TPF forces had regained control of Mekelle and its airport after the TDF withdrew from the city following its encirclement the previous day.[footnote 41]

2.3.7 On 24 September 2026, AFP reported that the TPLF stated it was in a ‘full-blown war’ with the federal government. The TPLF reportedly seized 3 airports from federal police on 23 September and launched attacks into Afar and Amhara, taking control of Abala on the Tigray/Afar border, with further fighting reported around Yallo in Afar and Weldiya in Amhara.[footnote 42]

2.3.8 On 25 September 2026, ACLED reported that fighting had expanded across several fronts in northern Ethiopia, including along the Tigray-Amhara border, in Afar and western Tigray, with repeated drone strikes reported across Tigray and northern Amhara. Fighting involving federal forces, the Amhara Fano National Movement and TDF was reported in North Wello and Wag Hamera zones in Amhara and around the Tekeze River, Tslimoy and May Gaba in western Tigray. Drone strikes were also reported in southern and north-western Tigray. The fighting resulted in the suspension of flights at Lalibela Airport in Amhara on 24 September 2026.[footnote 43]

2.3.9 On 28 September 2026 Ethiopia Observer reported the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) evacuated 161 people from Mekelle to Semera in Afar. The evacuees included Ethiopian Federal Police personnel and their families, Ethiopian Airlines staff and their families, African Union monitors, and members of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society.[footnote 44]

2.3.10 On 30 September 2026 ACLED reported that suicide drones suspected to be linked with the Alliance for Survival targeted ENDF facilities in Bishoftu, Kombolcha and Bahir Dar. In response to the attacks and wider security concerns, the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) announced a prohibition on the use of drones in Addis Ababa.[footnote 45]

2.3.11 On 1 October 2026 BBC reported explosions in Addis Ababa, including near the military headquarters and in the south of the city. A person linked to opposition forces claimed responsibility for alleged drone strikes, although there was no official confirmation of their cause, locations, or any casualties or damage.[footnote 46]

2.3.12 On 27 October 2026, CTP reported continued fighting between the ENDF and TDF across central and north-western Tigray. The forces clashed around Azeba, south-west of Adigrat, on 24 October and at Chila, north of the B30 between Axum and Shire, on 26 October. Northwest of Shire, the TDF had reportedly halted ENDF advances towards Sheraro, while artillery and small-arms fire was reported near Adi Hageray on 26 October. Federal forces also reportedly surrounded and captured TPLF central command member Major General Yohannes Woldegiyorgis (John Medid) and several other TDF commanders in Central Tigray on 26 October, although sources cited by CTP stated that they had surrendered.[footnote 47]

2.3.13 For background information on location, demography and language see CPIN: Tigrayans and the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front and Report of a fact-finding mission, Ethiopia: situation of the Tigrayans, December 2024

3. Key actors in the conflict

3.1 Overview

3.1.1 The SWP July 2026 report identified the following armed groups as key actors in the Tigray conflict:

ENDF: Ethiopian National Defense Forces (regular armed forces)

TDF: Tigray Defense Forces (Tigray’s regular security forces)

TIRA: Tigray Interim Regional Administration (stripped of power since May 2026)

TPLF: Tigray People’s Liberation Front (political party)

TPF: Tigray Peace Force (a splinter group of the TDF, pro-Addis Ababa).[footnote 48]

3.1.2 The Cedoca report of 22 July 2026 noted that the TPLF remained the central actor in Tigray and retained de facto influence within interim institutions and the security services. The TDF remained an important actor and sought to retain its autonomy and avoid integration into the ENDF or dissolution. The ENDF remained deployed along Tigray’s borders and retained an air-power advantage, while federal forces also relied on Tekeze Zeb [an Amhara militia based in Western Tigray] to restrict TDF movement towards Western Tigray. The Cedoca report also mentioned the TPF, or Hara Maret, comprised fighters and former officials dissatisfied with TPLF rule and sought to compel the TPLF to relinquish or share power. The report further noted alleged ENDF support to the TPF, reported contacts between the TPLF and Eritrea, and opportunistic cooperation between the TDF and Fano.[footnote 49]

3.3 Tigray Peoples’ Liberation Front (TPLF)

3.5 Tigray Peace Force (TPF)

3.5.1 The ICG February 2026 report observed:

‘This political rift [within the TPLF] has also emboldened an embryonic armed opposition group – the Tigray Peace Forces (TPF, known as Hara Meret in Tigrinya) – that split from the TDF earlier in 2025 and is active in the lands connecting Tigray to the Afar region. The group, which allegedly receives support from the federal government, has clashed with the TDF on several occasions. In early November, TPF-TDF skirmishes on the Tigray/Afar boundary reportedly prompted the federal government to carry out drone strikes on TDF units, which it claims had crossed into Afar territory.’[footnote 52]

3.5.2 The RVI March 2026 report stated:

‘The most consequential security development [in Tigray], … was the emergence of a new Tigrayan insurgent force. By 2025, dissident Tigrayans—including former mid-level TDF officers and disaffected local officials—lost faith in both TPLF and the interim setup. They united into the Tigray Peace Force (TPF), an armed resistance movement vowing to ‘liberate’ Tigray from TPLF’s one-party rule. The first hint of this came in April 2025 when Shewit Bitew, a young former TDF fighter, appeared in a widely circulated post announcing the TPF’s formation and denouncing TPLF leaders as corrupt authoritarian warlords. Shewit quickly became the TPF’s mouthpiece, framing it as a reformist movement seeking a more democratic and peaceful future for Tigray. Behind him stood Brigadier General Gebreegzabeher Beyene (‘Wedi Antiru’), a former TDF commander who had fallen out with the TPLF hierarchy.

‘TPF established bases in parts of Afar just across Tigray’s south-eastern border, with either overt or covert acceptance by federal authorities. By mid-2025 they had gathered a small but battle-hardened force. On 1 July 2025, the conflict within Tigray turned hot. A TPF unit crossed from Afar into Wejerat woreda in Southeastern Tigray zone and clashed with TSF units in what was the first armed confrontation between Tigrayan factions. The TSF repelled the incursion, but the brief firefight signalled a dangerous new phase—an incipient intra-Tigrayan conflict.’[footnote 53]

3.6.1 A June 2026 report by the Armed Conflict Location & Events Data Project (ACLED), an independent, impartial conflict monitor providing real-time data and analysis on violent conflict and protest in all countries and territories across the world[footnote 54] noted that Eritrea provided support to the TPLF and other opposition groups through an initiative referred to as Tsimdo, which ACLED described as a framework for cooperation among actors opposed to the Ethiopian federal government. According to the report a Tsimdo-linked conference was held in Port Sudan in May 2026 which reportedly brought together individuals associated with the Eritrean government, Sudanese actors, Amhara nationalists and other peripheral opposition groups, representing what ACLED characterised as an overt alignment of regional state and non-state actors against Addis Ababa.[footnote 55]

3.6.2 A July 2026 report by the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (SWP – the German Institute for International and Security Affairs), an independent German research institute specialising in international relations and security studies that provides policy analysis on global political and security developments[footnote 56] noted that relations between the TPLF and Eritrea have shifted significantly since the 2020–2022 conflict, with the parties reportedly engaging in cooperation based on shared opposition to the Ethiopian federal government. The report noted that Eritrea’s Tsimdo Selam initiative, launched in 2025 and presented by its organisers as a grassroots peace movement, is viewed by the Ethiopian government as part of a broader anti-government alliance involving the TPLF, Eritrea, Fano elements and other opposition actors.[footnote 57]

5. Conflict dynamics, incidents and fatalities

5.1 Overview

5.1.1 On 24 September 2026, Al Jazeera reported that ENDF stated it had killed at least 272 TPLF fighters during a counter-offensive in Amhara region. According to the ENDF, a further 260 TPLF fighters were wounded and several others captured. The military said the operation was launched in response to attacks by the TPLF and allied groups on several areas of North Wollo in the Amhara region, which borders Tigray, and resulted in significant personnel and equipment losses for the TPLF.[footnote 78] The source did not provide further information on ENDF casualties.

5.1.2 On 28 September 2026, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) reported a sharp increase in conflict-related casualties following the resumption of fighting between TPLF-aligned forces and the ENDF. MSF stated that the number of war-wounded patients treated at hospitals in Korem and Alamata increased from around 180 within 48 hours to more than 420 between 22 and 25 September 2026. In north-western Tigray, MSF also reported that more than 300 war-wounded patients had arrived at Suhul Hospital in Shire by 25 September. Owing to the security situation, MSF suspended activities at Alamata Hospital and redirected staff to support hospitals experiencing a significant influx of wounded patients​​.[footnote 79]

5.1.3 Between 1 January and 28 October 2026, Frontlines.et recorded 148 violent events and an estimated 239 to 242 fatalities in Tigray. Of these, Frontlines.et verified 92 events and 86 fatalities. A further 56 events and 156 fatalities were reported by one of the parties to the conflict but could not be independently verified by Frontlines.et. the 156 fatalities represents the upper estimate.[footnote 80]

5.2 ACLED data on political violence events and fatalities

5.2.1 The ACLED dataset records information on political violence which it defines as the use of force by a group for a political purpose, motivation, or effect. It records incidents as individual events involving identified actors occurring at a specific location and date.[footnote 81] Political violence events include battles, violence against civilians, explosions and remote violence and protests where there is intervention by another actor.[footnote 82]

5.2.2 Between 1 January and 21 October 2026 (latest available data), ACLED recorded 212 political violence incidents in Tigray that resulted in 253 fatalities. These comprised 111 battles (52.4%), 56 incidents of explosions and remote violence (26.4%), 44 incidents of violence against civilians (20.8%), and one riot (0.5%).[footnote 83]

6. Impact of conflict on civilians

6.1 Violence against civilians

6.1.1 A 25 September 2026 press release by the OHCHR stated: ‘UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk on Friday expressed alarm at the widening impact of the escalating fighting in Ethiopia on civilians. Airstrikes by the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), some carried out using drones, reportedly hit five schools in Tigray on 22 September, resulting in deaths and injuries. A mortar strike on 23 September in Kobo town in Amhara reportedly by the ENDF also resulted in civilian deaths.’[footnote 90]

6.1.2 On 25 September 2026, HRW reported that an apparent Ethiopian government airstrike struck a residential compound in the Daero neighbourhood of Mekelle on 20 August 2026. HRW reported that residents and witnesses said there were no Tigrayan fighters or other military personnel present at the compound or in the surrounding area before or after the strike. HRW further stated that it found no evidence to support reports that the attack was intended to target nearby Tigrayan military or civilian leaders. Victims were taken to Ayder Referral Hospital, where medical staff reported treating 13 people for injuries sustained in the strike, including three people with severe injuries and a 12-year-old girl who required surgery for a leg fracture.[footnote 91]

6.1.3 On 30 September 2026, BBC reported that hospital sources stated that at least 52 civilians were killed during three days of fighting in and around Alamata. A doctor at Alamata General Hospital told the BBC that heavy explosives and artillery were used during the fighting, some of which struck residential areas. The doctor stated that those killed included children, mothers, and cattle herders, and that 12 people were killed in a strike on the town’s marketplace. Separately, MSF reported that more than 700 war-wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supported in Tigray.[footnote 92]

6.5 Forced recruitment of civilians

6.5.1 On 28 May 2026, Addis Standard, an independent tri-lingual media outlet that publishes content in English, Afaan Oromoo and Amharic[footnote 99], reported allegations of forced recruitment of young people in several parts of Tigray, including Central and North Western Tigray, Adwa, and areas around Edaga Hamus Tsedya. Sources cited by the publication alleged that recruitment involved house-to-house searches and detention, including, in some cases, of relatives when targeted individuals could not be found. Recruits were reportedly taken to military training sites, and opposition groups alleged that forced conscription was occurring across Tigray. Addis Standard stated that it was unable to independently verify the allegation.[footnote 100]

6.5.2 On 5 June 2026, Addis Standard reported that Human Rights First Ethiopia (HRFE) alleged coercive recruitment across Tigray, including in Axum, Adwa, Shire, Adigrat, Mekelle and Wukro, as well as rural areas of the Central and North Western zones. Young men were reportedly detained at checkpoints, markets, transport terminals, and other public places and transferred to military training sites, while some individuals reportedly went into hiding or moved to avoid recruitment. Tigrayan opposition parties also criticised the reported recruitment, with the Tigray Independence Party accusing the TPLF and associated military structures of forced recruitment and of detaining relatives when targeted individuals could not be found.[footnote 101]

6.5.3 On 23 June 2026, Human Rights Watch (HRW) reported that local authorities and Tigrayan forces were implementing a mobilisation programme involving alleged forced recruitment, including of children. Former fighters were ordered to report to their units, while forces reportedly conducted door-to-door searches and mass roundups of potential recruits. HRW also received reports that relatives of those evading mobilisation were punished and that some residents had fled Tigray because of fears of forced recruitment and renewed hostilities.[footnote 102]

6.5.4 On 9 June 2026, Addis Standard reported that a draft proclamation prepared by Tigray’s reinstated pre-war council would establish a legal framework for mobilisation and make compliance with mobilisation orders compulsory. The draft reportedly provided penalties for evading military service, failing to report when summoned, assisting others to evade mobilisation or obstructing recruitment. It proposed prison sentences of up to 25 years for discouraging, intimidating, or misleading members of mobilisation structures, or encouraging them to abandon service or surrender weapons. Other offences could attract life imprisonment or, in the most serious cases, the death penalty. The draft was published amid reports of forced recruitment in parts of Tigray.[footnote 103]

6.5.5HRW also reported on the proclamation on 23 June 2026. According to the HRW report the proclamation established compulsory military mobilisation for those whose ‘health and age permit’ and contained what HRW described as vague and overly broad offences. It provided for the death penalty for some offences, including collaborating with the enemy or seriously threatening Tigray’s peace and security, prison sentences of up to 25 years for criticising or advocating resistance to the recruitment campaign, and fines of up to 50,000 Ethiopian Birr (approximately US$315) for evading mobilisation orders or deserting from service. HRW stated that the proclamation had reportedly been adopted without public scrutiny amid increasing tensions between the TPLF and the federal government.[footnote 104]

6.5.6 On 6 July 2026, HRW reported that Tigrayan authorities and forces had forcibly recruited civilians, including children as young as 15, since at least April 2026. HRW documented 6 cases based on interviews with 18 people and reported that former combatants and other men and boys were taken during street and market roundups, house-to-house searches and from gold-mining sites. Recruits were reportedly detained in administrative offices, jails, or schools before being transferred to military training camps, while former fighters were also returned to their units. HRW further reported that some people went into hiding or fled Tigray to avoid recruitment and that, in some cases, relatives of those evading service were detained.[footnote 105]

6.6 Conflict related arrest and detention

6.6.1 On 10 February 2026, UN News reported that the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, stated that both the TSF and the ENDF had reportedly arrested civilians suspected of having links to the opposing side. According to the High Commissioner, such arrests formed part of ongoing human rights concerns in the context of tensions and insecurity in Tigray.[footnote 106]

6.6.2 HRW April 2026 report stated that security forces and local militia groups in Western Tigray, including the Tekeze Zeb militia, continued to arbitrarily detain Tigrayans in police stations and at Bet Hintset prison in Humera. According to HRW, arbitrary arrests increased following clashes in Tselemti in January 2026, with reports that men and individuals returning from other parts of Tigray were particularly affected.[footnote 107]

6.6.3 ACLED also recorded abductions/forced disappearance which were linked to forced recruitment and conscription. Between 1 January and 21 October 2026, ACLED recorded 29 abduction/forced-disappearance events in Tigray between 2 April and 2 October 2026. Twenty-seven of these events were explicitly linked in the notes to forced recruitment or conscription. The incidents were attributed overwhelmingly to the TDF, with one event led by the Tigray State Police. The event narratives contain numerical references to approximately 1,074 abducted persons, although only 834 can be supported using strict lower-bound counts. The actual number of victims was higher because several events involved ‘hundreds’, ‘several’, or otherwise unspecified numbers of people. Additionally, ACLED recorded 10 arrest events 3 of which were linked to recruitment or conscription. In total 10 individuals were arrested: 9 after allegedly opposing, criticizing, or discouraging recruitment efforts, including 7 members of the Salsay Woyane Tigray Party and 2 senior Orthodox archbishops and the other, a hospital executive on allegations of assisting recruitment for the TPF. Two of the recruitment-related arrests were attributed to the Tigray state police and one to the TDF.[footnote 108]

6.7 Population displacement

6.7.1 The number of internally displaced persons increased from an estimated 710,000 individuals in June 2025[footnote 109] to approximately 761,284 at the end of July 2026.[footnote 110]

6.7.2 The February 2026 Global Protection Cluster monthly overview reported that an estimated 2,500 people had been displaced in Tigray’s North Western Zone and 37,000 in the South Eastern Zone. Of those displaced in the South Eastern Zone, around 30,000 had reportedly returned to their areas of origin, while approximately 7,000 remained displaced and in urgent need of assistance.[footnote 111]

6.7.3 On 27 April 2026, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) reported that renewed hostilities in Alamata, Raya Alamata and Raya Bala (Southern Tigray) in February 2026 resulted in the displacement of an estimated 78,450 people to Kobo in North Wollo Zone.[footnote 112]

6.8 Civilian infrastructure and access to services

6.8.1 The Protection Cluster reported in March 2026 that humanitarian access in Tigray had deteriorated due to insecurity, reduced operational movement, and severe fuel and cash shortages. The report noted that fuel shortages restricted humanitarian operations and affected the populations’ access to services, while bank withdrawal restrictions in Tigray impeded cash-based assistance programmes. Despite these constraints, protection partners reached 46,704 people through awareness activities and provided over ETB 5.7 million in cash assistance to 759 vulnerable women and girls.[footnote 113] The situation remained the same in July 2026 with the Protection Cluster reporting that insecurity and continued fuel and cash shortages were affecting humanitarian operations, while the non-payment of salaries, including those of teachers, continued to disrupt service delivery.[footnote 114]

6.8.2 According to the World Food Programme (WFP) August 2026 situation report, insecurity in Tigray continued to hamper humanitarian operations, constraining supply routes and delaying the timely delivery of assistance.[footnote 115]

6.8.3 On 10 September 2026, the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect (GCR2P), an international NGO that advocates on atrocity prevention and response[footnote 116], reported that, following the resumption of fighting on 1 August 2026, the Ethiopian government had reportedly carried out near-daily drone strikes in Tigray, affecting civilians and civilian infrastructure, including schools, farms and residential homes.[footnote 117]

6.8.4 On 21 September 2026, Addis Standard reported that a humanitarian aid truck carrying 41 metric tonnes of food assistance for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Sheraro, north-western Tigray, was reportedly struck by a drone the previous day. The strike reportedly injured a 13-year-old girl and destroyed the food consignment, which was intended for an IDP camp hosting more than 56,000 displaced people.[footnote 118]

6.8.5 On 28 September 2026, the UN Secretary-General’s Spokesperson reported that worsening insecurity across northern Ethiopia was increasing humanitarian needs and disrupting humanitarian operations. Humanitarian access to Tigray was severely restricted by disrupted telecommunications, suspended flights, and restrictions on key roads, limiting the movement of humanitarian personnel, relief supplies, and civilians. Funding shortages had placed further pressure on the response, with several humanitarian partners scaling back or suspending operations despite increasing needs.[footnote 119]

6.8.6 On 8 October 2026, The New Humanitarian, an independent, non-profit newsroom that reports on humanitarian crises, conflicts, and disasters worldwide[footnote 120] reported a breakdown in law and order in Mekelle following the withdrawal of TPLF forces and the advance of federal troops. Armed groups reportedly looted civilian and humanitarian facilities, including government and post offices, humanitarian premises, and aid warehouses, resulting in the loss of vehicles, medical equipment, and relief supplies. The Organisation for Social Services, Health and Development (OSSHD-Ethiopia) reportedly lost around 60 computers and tablets, nearly all its vehicles, approximately US$1 million of non-food items and tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of medical equipment intended for its clinic in Mekelle. The source reported that police had withdrawn as federal forces approached, leaving no effective policing presence to maintain public order.[footnote 121]

6.9 Freedom of movement

6.9.1 HRW reported in April 2026 that freedom of movement for Tigrayans in Western Tigray remained restricted. According to the report Tigrayans were required to obtain temporary travel permits from local authorities to travel outside their immediate locality, including for employment, medical treatment, and family visits. HRW stated that permits were generally limited in duration and geographical scope, with travel documents reviewed by the organisation indicating that movement outside authorised areas could result in prosecution. The report also described the presence of official and ad hoc checkpoints operated by security forces, where individuals were reportedly required to present identification documents or travel permits. HRW further reported that some interviewees limited their movements because of concerns about arrest, detention, or harassment.[footnote 122]

6.9.2 On 20 April 2026, Ethiopia Today, citing reporting by Wazema, reported restrictions on the movement of young people attempting to leave Tigray. According to the source, authorities had established checkpoints on routes leading to the Amhara and Afar regions, where vehicles carrying groups of young people were reportedly intercepted and turned back. The same source reported that the Tigray Police Commission stated that the police had intercepted and returned more than 150 people in one week and that 171 individuals had been detained while attempting to leave the region. The source stated that concerns about recruitment by Tigrayan forces and fears of renewed conflict were among the reasons cited by some young people for leaving the region.[footnote 123]

6.9.3 On 25 September 2026, the Associated Press (AP) reported that roads connecting Tigray with the neighbouring Afar region had been closed to civilian traffic. AP also reported that air travel to Tigray had been suspended after TPLF-affiliated fighters reportedly seized Mekelle airport, leading Ethiopian Airlines to cancel flights to and from the region.[footnote 124]

6.9.4 On 25 September 2026, the Ethiopia Human Rights Commission (EHRC) reported that flights to and from Tigray had been suspended after TPLF-affiliated fighters captured the airports at Mekelle, Shire and Axum. EHRC further reported that land routes linking Tigray to other parts of Ethiopia had been completely cut off, affecting freedom of movement and disrupting the supply of basic goods and services triggering subsequent price inflation.[footnote 125]
